title: God is known by the mind and seen by a pure heart
source_text: Οἰόμενος δ᾿ ἡμᾶς διὰ τὸ γνῶναι καὶ ἰδεῖν τὸν θεὸν πρεσβεύειν τὰ περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως συνείρει ἑαυτῷ ἃ βούλεται καὶ τοιαῦτά φησιν· ὅταν δὴ πάντοθεν ἐξείργωνται καὶ διελέγχωνται, πάλιν ὥσπερ οὐδὲν ἀκηκοότες ἐπανίασιν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἐρώτημα· πῶς οὖν γνῶμεν καὶ ἴδωμεν τὸν θεόν; καὶ πῶς ἴωμεν πρὸς αὐτόν; ἴστω οὖν ὁ βουλόμενος ὅτι, κἂν εἰς ἄλλα δεώμεθα σώματος τῷ ἐν τόπῳ σωματικῷ τυγχάνειν, καὶ τοιούτου, ὁποία ἐστὶν ἡ φύσις τοῦ σωματικοῦ τόπου, καὶ δεόμενοι τοῦ σώματος ἐπενδυώμεθα τῷ σκήνει τὰ προειρημένα, ἀλλ᾿ εἰς γνῶσίν γε θεοῦ σώματος οὐδαμῶς χρῄζομεν. τὸ γὰρ γινῶσκον θεὸν οὐκ ὀφθαλμός ἐστι σώματος ἀλλὰ νοῦς, ὁρῶν τὸ „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα“ τοῦ κτίσαντος καὶ τὸ δυνάμενον γινώσκειν θεὸν προνοίᾳ θεοῦ ἀνειληφώς. καὶ τὸ ὁρῶν δὲ θεὸν καθαρά ἐστι καρδία, ἀφ᾿ ἧς οὐκέτι „ἐξέρχονται διαλογισμοὶ πονηροὶ,“ οὐ „φόνοι,“ οὐ „μοιχεῖαι,“ οὐ „πορνεῖαι,“ οὐ „κλοπαὶ,“ οὐ „ψευδομαρτυρίαι,“ οὐ „βλασφημίαι,“ οὐκ „ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρὸς“ οὐδ᾿ ἄλλο τι τῶν ἀτόπων· δι᾿ ἃ λέγεται· „μακάριοι οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ, ὅτι αὐτοὶ τὸν θεὸν ὄψονται.“ ἐπεὶ δ᾿ οὐκ αὐτάρκης ἡ ἡμετέρα προαίρεσις πρὸς τὸ πάντῃ „καθαρὰν“ ἔχειν τὴν „καρδίαν,“ ἀλλὰ θεοῦ ἡμῖν δεῖ, κτίζοντος αὐτὴν τοιαύτην, διὰ τοῦτο λέγεται ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐπιστημόνως εὐχομένου· „καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοὶ ὁ θεός.“
pass_a_gloss: Supposing (οἴομαι) that we hold in honour (πρεσβεύω) the things about the resurrection for the sake of knowing (γνῶναι) and seeing (ἰδεῖν) God, he strings together (συνείρω) for himself what he wishes and says such things: ‘whenever they are shut out (ἐξείργω) on all sides and refuted (διελέγχω), again as if having heard nothing they come back (ἐπάνειμι) to the same question (ἐρώτημα): “how then may we know and see God? and how may we go (ἴωμεν) to him?”’ Let him who wishes know, then, that even if for other things we need a body by being in a bodily place, and such a body as is the nature of the bodily place, and needing the body we put on over (ἐπενδύομαι) the tent the things said before, yet for knowledge (γνῶσις) of God we in no way need (χρῄζω) a body. For what knows God is not an eye (ὀφθαλμός) of the body but mind (νοῦς), seeing (ὁρῶν) the ‘according to the image (κατ᾿ εἰκόνα)’ of the one who created (κτίζω), and having received (ἀναλαμβάνω) by God’s providence (πρόνοια) the capacity to know God. And what sees God is a pure heart (καθαρὰ καρδία), from which no longer come out evil reasonings (διαλογισμοὶ πονηροί), not murders (φόνοι), not adulteries (μοιχεῖαι), not fornications (πορνεῖαι), not thefts (κλοπαί), not false testimonies (ψευδομαρτυρίαι), not blasphemies (βλασφημίαι), not an evil eye, nor any other of the out-of-place things (ἄτοπα); because of which it is said: ‘blessed (μακάριοι) the pure in heart, because they shall see God.’ But since our choice (προαίρεσις) is not self-sufficient (αὐτάρκης) to have the heart wholly pure, but we need God, creating it such, therefore it is said by the one praying knowingly (ἐπιστημόνως): ‘a pure heart create in me, O God.’
pass_b_english: Supposing that we hold the doctrine of the resurrection for the sake of knowing and seeing God, Celsus strings together whatever he likes, and says something like this: “When they are shut out on every side and refuted, they come back again, as if they had heard nothing, to the same question: ‘How then are we to know and see God? And how are we to go to him?’”

Let anyone who wishes know, then, that even if for other purposes we need a body, because we are in a bodily place, and a body suited to the nature of that bodily place, and even if, since we need the body, we put on over the tent what we have described, yet for the knowledge of God we have no need of a body at all. For what knows God is not the eye of the body but the mind, which sees what is “in the image” (Genesis 1:26–27) of the Creator, and which by the providence of God has received the power to know God.

And what sees God is a pure heart, from which there no longer “come forth evil thoughts,” no “murders,” no “adulteries,” no “fornications,” no “thefts,” no “false witness,” no “blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19), no “evil eye” (Mark 7:22), nor anything else that is wrong. That is why it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). But since our own free choice is not enough for us to have a heart wholly “pure,” and we need God to create it so, the one who prays with understanding says: “Create in me a pure heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10).

choices.choice: The Greek subject of the first sentence is unnamed (οἰόμενος); ‘Celsus’ is supplied for clarity. Celsus’s words run from ‘When they are shut out’ to ‘go to him’, with the Christians’ question as he frames it nested in single marks. Syntax: in νοῦς, ὁρῶν τὸ ‘κατ᾿ εἰκόνα’ τοῦ κτίσαντος καὶ τὸ δυνάμενον γινώσκειν θεὸν προνοίᾳ θεοῦ ἀνειληφώς, the order participle + object on each side of καί is taken at face value: the mind sees what is ‘in the image’ of the Creator, and has received by God’s providence the power to know God. A possible alternative takes both neuter objects with ἀνειληφώς (‘which sees, since it has received the image and the power to know God’); the doctrine stated is the same. The vice list follows Matthew 15:19 in order; ‘evil eye’ comes from Mark 7:22. Psalm 50:12 LXX = Psalm 51:10 English. ‘What we have described’ refers to the garments of chapter 32.

Looked again at the doubtful syntax: ὁρῶν now takes its following object (‘the mind, which sees what is “in the image” of the Creator, and which … has received the power to know God’); the earlier reading is kept in the notes as the alternative
‘we need God, who creates it such’ to ‘we need God to create it so’ (κτίζοντος expresses what we need God for)
Speaker frame checked (Celsus in double marks, the Christians’ question as he frames it in single marks); Matthew 15:19, Mark 7:22, Matthew 5:8, Psalm 50:12 LXX = 51:10 verified

choices.choice: 7.33: the Greek around νοῦς, ὁρῶν τὸ κατ᾿ εἰκόνα ... ἀνειληφώς can be read two ways. Either gives the same doctrine; the chosen reading and the other one are both in translator_notes.
